conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing why you came in tonight. You’ve been having abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting again—same as before. Can you tell me more about how you’re feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain is across both upper sides, not just one. It’s about a 6 out of 10 now, but was worse earlier. I’ve also had chills and loose stools, but no blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. In the ER, they gave you fluids, Zofran for nausea, and Dilaudid for pain. Your labs show your hemoglobin dropped a bit since your last admission, but it’s stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was admitted at U Mass last week too. They said my hemoglobin was 23, so I got a blood transfusion. And they did an EGD—found ulcers in my esophagus, not bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that in your report. Since the ulcers aren’t bleeding, we’ll keep you on Nexium to help them heal. We also checked your lipase and liver tests—both normal, so no sign of pancreatitis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had so many CT scans, and they never find pancreatitis. But I still get these episodes. I also have this rash on my belly—no itching, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I checked your skin—it looks non-specific, not concerning for infection or vasculitis. Speaking of which, your rheumatology consult two weeks ago didn’t find evidence to support vasculitis, so we’re not restarting methotrexate or Plaquenil.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was supposed to have a parotid gland biopsy to check for Sjogren’s, but I canceled. My PCP said I should be off methotrexate and Plaquenil for a month first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, we checked with rheumatology and your PCP—only one week off those meds is needed. So you can schedule the biopsy sooner. It’s important to confirm or rule out Sjogren’s, especially with your family history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that. I’ll call my PCP. I also haven’t started with the pain clinic or psychiatry yet. My PCP said they’d help set that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a key part of your care. Chronic pain and anxiety often go together, and a coordinated team can help more than repeated ER visits. We recommend connecting with both services soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking amitriptyline again. My PCP said not to stop it. But I remember last time, GI said it might worsen gut motility?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a concern. But since your PCP advised continuing it, we’ll keep it for now. Just know it’s something to discuss with them—especially if nausea or bloating gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You slept well, and your repeat labs look stable. Your hemoglobin is 10.2, which is low but not dropping. You’ve been off IV meds overnight and seem comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Can I try eating? I’ve been on IV fluids, but I’d like to go home today if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we can advance your diet. But more importantly—we talked about your pain management. IV Dilaudid isn’t solving the root issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but my clinic can’t access my Port-a-cath after hours. That’s why I end up here—I can’t get pain relief at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. But long-term, we need a plan. We’re discharging your narcotics and focusing on oral meds. You’re on Nexium twice daily, and now we’re adding Emend as a rescue for nausea if Zofran doesn’t work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other meds? I never got the Emend last time—it had to be special ordered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This time, you’ll get a prescription to fill at discharge. We’re also adjusting your escitalopram to 20 mg total—split into morning and night—for better anxiety control. Betaxolol is now 20 mg daily, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. So I can go home if I keep down food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll go home today. But please follow up with your PCP, get the parotid biopsy scheduled, and push for the pain and psychiatric referrals. That’s how we’ll make progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything. It helps to know we’re not missing something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Your pain is real, even if we haven’t found a clear cause. The goal now is managing it better outside the hospital. We’ll send all instructions to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well on liquids. We’re switching you to a soft diet. Once you finish this meal, and if you feel stable, we can discharge you in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll eat slowly and let you know how I feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the meal well. I’ve reviewed your discharge plan. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your medication list and follow-up instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow up with my team and keep working on this.
